Its strings vibrate to produce rich overtones, which gives a crystalline sound. The resonating chamber is designed so that the sound sustains and rings well, with a slight tremor, which is exactly the effect its name suggests. Against the warm heaviness of a traditional guitar the tremoloa is lighter and more floating; against the harp it sounds more modern and more rhythmic. This character makes it particularly suited to evoking the exotic flavour of Hawaiian music, and in contemporary experimental music it can create a psychedelic, expressive atmosphere.

The tremoloa is a chordophone of the fretless zither family made in the United States, Hornbostel–Sachs number 314.122-6, mass-produced from the 1920s as Hawaiian music became popular and continuing into the 1950s. A weighted roller runs along the melody string, steadied by a swinging lever; after the string is plucked the roller is moved to make a vibrato, imitating the sound of the Hawaiian steel guitar. There are also four chord groups, C, G, F and D major, for strummed harmony. Broken Social Scene use it in the song 'Tremoloa Debut', and The Magnetic Fields use it occasionally on the album 69 Love Songs.

The neck is mostly a harder wood such as mahogany or maple, for stability. The sounding strings are steel or nylon, with strong tension and durability. The strings carry metal tuning pins and machine heads made of a copper or nickel alloy for corrosion resistance. The surface may be protected with a traditional paint or varnish.
